Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 3:20: There is yet another aspect of fear: when a person reflects on the abundant goodness of the Creator, blessed be He, toward him, as the pious author of Chovot HaLevavot, peace be upon him, elaborated (Gate of Trust, chapter 6), that the Creator's goodness to man exceeds anything a person could do in all his days, for all his days and nights would not suffice to repay even one of the Creator's kindnesses toward him, as will be explained in part in the Gate of Love from what our Sages, of blessed memory, explained. And if a person sins while the Holy One, blessed be He, continues to bestow goodness upon him, he is thereby consuming his merits in this world and his merits are diminishing, as our father Jacob, peace be upon him, said (Genesis 32:11) "I am unworthy of all the kindnesses and all the truth," and Rashi explains: "my merits have been diminished by the kindnesses and truth You have done for me, and therefore I fear that since You promised me, I may have become sullied by sin, which may cause me to be delivered into Esau's hand" - so far. So too the Targum renders, "my merits have grown small," etc. Therefore one must feel shame and not be ungrateful for the goodness of the Creator, blessed be He, toward him.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 3:21: Further, a third aspect our Sages, of blessed memory, explained in the Sifrei, quoted in the Yalkut (Yalkut Kohelet, remez 971), on the verse (Ecclesiastes 5:1) "for God is in heaven," etc. - their words: "'For God is in heaven' - who does not know that the Holy One, blessed be He, is in heaven and human beings are on earth? Rather, Solomon said: since even the weakest of the weak above is victorious over the mighty [below] - weak from below, and above, mighty over the mighty - how much more so [should this teach us caution]. And so it says (Deuteronomy 32:6) 'is this how you repay the Lord?'" - so far, as relevant to us.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 3:22: Through this passage one verse of David the king, peace be upon him, is explained (Psalms 47:3) "for the Lord is Most High, awesome, a great King over all the earth." The meaning, based on what was said in this passage - that one who is above is victorious over the mighty who are below - is: "for the Lord is Most High, awesome" - because He is Most High, one must fear Him; and how much more so is He "a great King over all the earth," meaning that He watches over every detail of the world, and He is called King because He judges the world with judgment, for the world stands only on judgment, and a person is judged every day, as our Sages, of blessed memory, explained (Rosh Hashanah 16a). This will be further elaborated on, with the Lord's help.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 3:23: Further, a fourth aspect explained by Rashbi, peace be upon him, in the Tikkunim (5b), concerning the fear that comes from shame - his words: "The eighth level in the fear of the Lord is that a person should have shame of countenance: whoever has shame of countenance, that he not commit a transgression that would come to his hand, because of fear of the Holy One, blessed be He, as though the world were created through him - and therefore [it is called] 'bereishit' [in the beginning], 'fears shame' [yare boshet]. Behold, fear and shame are one and the same."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 3:24: And he says further on: "and further, shame of countenance [leads] to the Garden of Eden, and brazenness of countenance to Gehinnom; those who commit transgression with a high hand and have no shame of countenance before the Holy One, blessed be He, of whom it is said (Isaiah 6:3) 'the whole earth is full of His glory,' and of whom it is said (Proverbs 20:27) 'He searches all the innermost chambers, He sees the kidneys and the heart' - and humility is bound up with fear, as it is said (ibid. 22:4) 'the reward of humility is the fear of the Lord' - whoever has the fear of the Lord within him is brought to humility, which is the supernal Shechinah, to whom the fear of the Lord is joined as its 'heel.' This is the level of Moses, of whom it is said (Numbers 12:3) 'and the man Moses was very humble,' and because fear is joined to her as a 'heel,' the masters of the Mishnah established, 'fear is a minor matter compared to Moses'" - so far, as relevant to us.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 3:25: We find, then, that one must fear and feel shame before the Shechinah that is before him, for "the whole earth is full of His glory," and not transgress any of His commandments, blessed be He. So too the author of Chovot HaLevavot wrote (Gate of the Service of God, chapter 5); the pious one said: "Do not defy your Master while He watches over you."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 3:26: Now, the fear from this aspect is the fear of which the verse speaks (Exodus 20:17) "and that His fear may be upon your faces, so that you do not sin"; and so our Sages, of blessed memory, explained in the Mechilta, and likewise in Nedarim, chapter 2 (20a) - their words: "It is taught: 'and that His fear may be upon your faces' - this is shame; 'so that you do not sin' - this teaches that shame brings one to fear of sin. From this they said: it is a good sign for a person to be bashful. Others say: any person who feels shame will not quickly sin, and whoever has no shame of countenance, it is certain that his ancestors did not stand at Mount Sinai" - so far. They were compelled to interpret "fear" as "shame" because it says "upon your faces," for fear is only in the heart, as was explained above; and also, what does "so that you do not sin" mean - is it because the fear is on their faces that they will not sin? For this reason, both interpretations reasoned carefully and said that the fear which is shame on the face brings one to fear of sin.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 3:27: Shame is when a person feels embarrassed in matters of the world before another person and is modest in his conduct; likewise, when spoken to, he feels shame and does not look directly into the other's face - this indicates that the awe of the King of the world's sovereignty is upon him, and likewise his speech is gentle. This is the matter of shame, and from it fear of sin follows for him. And in the Tikkunim (136a): "faces reddened with shame, who feel embarrassment before Heaven - they are those who fear God" - so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 3:28: The matter of fear of sin is explained by Rabbeinu Nissim, peace be upon him, on the Beraita of Rabbi Pinchas (Avodah Zarah 20b): "Watchfulness leads to alacrity," etc., and it says there, "holiness leads to fear of sin, fear of sin leads to humility," etc. The explanation of "fear of sin" is that one fears sin as one fears an enemy, in such a way that this is an additional level in a person - that fear is so firmly established in his heart that he fears the sin itself and distances himself far from it.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 3:29: It seems to me that "fear of sin" means that he fears sinning because of the disgrace of the sin itself - for how could he sin before the King who is before him, and bring before Him refuse and transgressions, since the kelipah [shell] is a diminution taken from holiness, from the language of (I Kings 1:21) "I and my son Solomon will be counted as sinners."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 3:30: In Ra'aya Meheimna (portion of Ki Teitzei, 278b) it is explained that "fear of sin" is the supernal Mother, Teshuvah [Repentance] - his words: "The commandment is the soul [nefesh], the spirit [ruach] is the Torah, and therefore they established: it is not the study that is essential but the deed. And elsewhere they said: whoever's fear of sin precedes his wisdom, his wisdom endures; and whoever's wisdom precedes his fear of sin, his wisdom does not endure. Fear of sin is the supernal Mother, Teshuvah; wisdom is the supernal Father. When the small Heh, which is the commandment [mitzvah], precedes, the Torah, which is Vav, rests upon it; and when fear precedes wisdom, which is the supernal Heh, wisdom, which is Yud, rests upon it, and it is called 'son' - hence 'you are sons to the Lord your God'" - so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 3:31: We find, according to this, that the shame a person feels at sinning on account of the Shechinah - which is the very thing explained in the Tikkunim - brings one to attain a higher level, which is fear of sin; this is what is explained in the Tikkunim (5b), that fear is bound up with humility, for from this follows that a person becomes humble, not answering back even when insulted, since he fears and feels shame to respond before the King who is before him - like Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, of whom it is said (Numbers 12:3) "and the man Moses was very humble," as is explained there in the Tikkunim in the passage quoted. This is [the meaning of] "the reward of humility is the fear of the Lord" (Proverbs 22:4) - meaning that the end of the levels of humility is the fear of the Lord, just as the heel is the end of a person's body; and since it says that the end of humility is the fear of the Lord, it appears there is a bond between them, joining both as one, this one being the end and that one the beginning; and the bond between them is certainly the fear that comes from shame of countenance.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 3:32: This aspect of fear is explained in the Zohar (Naso 145a) - their words: "Rabbi Yitzchak opened (Psalms 103:17) 'but the kindness of the Lord is from everlasting to everlasting upon those who fear Him' - how great is fear before the Holy One, blessed be He, for within fear is included humility, and within humility is included piety. We find that whoever has fear of sin has them all included within him, and whoever does not fear Heaven has neither humility nor piety" - so far his words. More will be explained regarding fear of sin in the next chapter, with the Lord's help.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:1: This chapter will explain how many aspects there are to the matter of fear of sin. First, one must fear that no sin come to his hand, even unintentionally, the reason being that since the soul is a fine and spiritual being, emanated from a lofty place, anything a person blemishes, even unintentionally, darkens the soul - like the parable of one who spills a jug of oil or ink on his clean white garments, even unintentionally: the stain darkens that garment. Concerning this Solomon the king, peace be upon him, said (Ecclesiastes 9:8) "let your garments always be white, and let oil not be lacking on your head."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:2: They were stringent about this and said in the Tanchuma (portion of Vayikra), quoted in the Yalkut (portion of Vayikra, remez 464), on the verse (Leviticus 4:2) "and if a soul sins unintentionally" - their words: "To what can this be compared? To two men who sinned against the king, one a commoner and one a member of the palace household. He saw that both had committed the same sin; he pardoned the commoner but gave the palace member a formal indictment. The king's household said to him: both sinned the same sin - the commoner you pardoned, and the palace member you gave a formal indictment? He said to them: the commoner I pardoned because he does not know the customs of royalty, but the palace member stands with me every day and knows the customs of royalty, and [yet] he sins. So too, the body is the 'commoner' - (Genesis 2:7) 'and the Lord God formed man,' etc. - while the soul is the 'palace member,' from above - 'and He breathed into his nostrils the breath of life' - and both sin. Therefore Scripture expresses wonder: 'if a soul sins.' What does 'unintentionally, from among all the commandments' mean? To teach you that whoever sins unintentionally is as though he transgressed the commandment of the Lord [deliberately], as it says (Numbers 15:22) 'and if you err and do not perform all the commandments,' and it says (Psalms 19:13) 'who can discern errors... also keep back Your servant from willful sins' - an error in learning becomes tantamount to a willful sin" - so far, as relevant to us. Here it is explicitly stated that the punishment for the soul is because it was the 'palace member,' a member of the household of the supreme King, and it knows the customs of royalty, which is the Torah, taught to it before it comes into the world.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:3: What is said, "it stands with me every day," refers to the fact that every night the soul ascends above to report on a person's deeds, as our Sages, of blessed memory, explained (Tanna DeVei Eliyahu Zuta, chapter 1), on "while you lie in your bosom, guard the openings of your mouth" (Micah 7:5); and according to its merit, so does it see above, and so is it taught, as we shall elaborate further on, with the Lord's help.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:4: It may also be said that "it stands with me" refers to engaging in Torah study, for one who studies Torah stands with the Holy One, blessed be He, as our Sages, of blessed memory, explained (Tanna DeVei Eliyahu Rabbah, chapter 18) on (Lamentations 2:19) "pour out your heart like water before the presence of the Lord": the Holy One, blessed be He, sits opposite the one who reads and studies, reading and studying with him, etc., and from this he knows the customs of royalty. The first explanation seems to me the primary one.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:5: According to this midrash, the body has no punishment [of its own]. But there are those who disagree, in Midrash Vayikra Rabbah (4:5), saying that the soul and the body are both punished together, and they bring the parable of the lame man and the blind man for this; and concerning this it is said (Psalms 50:4) "He calls to the heavens above and to the earth, to judge His people" - "He calls to the heavens above" to bring the soul, "and to the earth" to bring the body, "and afterward, to judge His people" together. So too our Sages, of blessed memory, explained (Sanhedrin 91b); this view appears to be the more accepted one.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:6: Let us return to our subject: it is proven from the words of the midrash that a person is punished in two respects. The first, because his soul is spiritual, a king's child, and it was fitting for it to gaze upon the glory of the supreme King, and even if he sinned unintentionally he is punished as though he had sinned deliberately, since an error in learning becomes tantamount to a willful sin. And what it says, "and so it says, 'and if you err and do not perform all the commandments,'" is to be understood by what is said in Ra'aya Meheimna, quoted in the portion of Naso (124a) - their words: "and whoever fulfills one commandment properly, it is as though he fulfilled all two hundred and forty-eight positive commandments, for there is no commandment that does not comprise all two hundred and forty-eight" - so far. Now, from what constitutes fulfillment we know the punishment for transgression, for one who transgresses one commandment is as though he transgresses them all, and this is [the meaning of] "and if you err and do not perform all the commandments."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:7: The Zohar (Vayikra 13a) explains, on this verse (Leviticus 4:2) "if a soul sins unintentionally," a matter relevant to our discussion, and I have chosen to quote it, although it is lengthy, because of its great value for the matter of fear and repentance; it is along the lines of what is explained in the midrash we quoted - his words: "'If a soul sins' - Rabbi Yosi opened (Song of Songs 2:17) 'until the day breathes and the shadows flee,' etc. How much do human beings need to be careful of their sins, not to sin before their Master! For every single day a herald goes forth and calls: awaken, people of the world, and be ashamed before the Holy King; awaken, be careful of your sins; awaken, holy soul that was placed within you from a holy, supernal place. For we learn that at the time the Holy One, blessed be He, brings forth the soul to descend into human beings, He makes it testify with many oaths and many pledges, to keep His commandments. Not only that, but He causes it to pass through a thousand and eight worlds to delight in and see the glory of those who occupy themselves with the Torah; it goes forth and stands before the King in a garment of glory, and afterward, in the image of this world, in that supernal light, it gazes upon the glory of the King every day, and it is crowned with several crowns. When the time comes for it to descend into the world, it makes an abode in the Garden of Eden for thirty days, to see the glory of the Master of the righteous, and it ascends to its place, and after this it descends into the world; the Holy King crowns it with seven crowns until it comes and enters into a person's body, and it returns into this world and occupies itself with its darkness. The Torah is astonished at it and says: and all this glory and all this perfection which the supreme King has bestowed upon this soul, and it has hidden itself before Him - 'if a soul sins' - how could this be, that it sins? Rabbi Yosi said: 'if a soul sins' - I return to the verse 'until the day breathes' - this is advice for this soul, to be careful of its sins and to repent, to purify itself, 'until the day breathes' - before the day of this world breathes its last and that mighty day comes when the King demands judgment of it, to leave this world."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:8: "And the shadows flee" - this is the secret the colleagues speak of, that when the time comes for a person to leave the world, his shadow departs from him; this is [the meaning of] (Song of Songs 2:17) "until the day breathes" - until the day breathes its last, [i.e.] for him to leave this world, "and the shadows flee" - his shadow departs, and he sits before his Master.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:9: Rabbi Elazar said: a person has two shadows while he exists [in this world], one large and one small, and they are found together; thus is a person in his existence, and therefore it is written "and the shadows flee" [in the plural]. At that time a person must examine his deeds and set them right before his Master, and confess concerning them, since the Holy One, blessed be He, is called "Merciful and Gracious," and accepts those who repent before Him. This is [the meaning of] "until the day breathes and the shadows flee" - since those shadows depart from him and he is caught in the collar [i.e., seized to give account], it is a kind of repentance, though not as complete as it would have been at the time he existed [fully, in health]. And Solomon the king proclaimed and said (Ecclesiastes 12:1) "remember your Creator in the days of your youth, before the evil days come," etc. And therefore "until the day breathes" - a person needs to set his deeds right, for when his days draw near to depart from the world, the Holy One, blessed be He, is astonished at him and says, "if a soul sins" - and "hears a voice of adjuration" (Leviticus 5:1) - for I already adjured it with an oath by My Name not to be false to Me, and I made it testify when it descended into the world. And it - the soul itself - is certainly a witness, from the many times I made it testify to keep the commandments; therefore, since a person is [himself] a witness at the time he returns before the King - "whether he saw or knew" (ibid.) - either he saw those sins he committed and gazes upon them, or he clearly knows in the matter that he transgressed his Master's command - "if he does not speak up" - if he does not confess them before his Master - what is written when he leaves this world? "He shall bear his iniquity" - and when he bears his iniquity, how will they open a gate for him, and how will he stand before his Master? Therefore it is written 'if a soul sins'" - so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:10: Here it is explained in this passage how much the Holy One, blessed be He, wonders at the soul when it did not do the will of its Maker, since it stood above and saw the King's palace and its customs; this is along the lines of what was said in the first passage from the Tanchuma we quoted at the beginning of the chapter.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:11: Along these lines it is further explained in the midrash, quoted in the Yalkut (portion of Ha'azinu, remez 942), on the verse (Deuteronomy 32:2) "my teaching shall drop like the rain" - their words: "And so Rabbi Simai used to say: all creatures created from the heavens have both their soul and body from the heavens, and all creatures created from the earth have both their soul and body from the earth, except for man, whose soul is from the heavens and whose body is from the earth. Therefore, if man performs Torah and does the will of his Father in heaven, behold, he is like the beings above, as it is said (Psalms 82:6) 'I said, you are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High.' If he does not perform Torah and does not do the will of his Father in heaven, behold, he is like the beings below, as it is said (ibid.) 'nevertheless, you shall die like man.' Rabbi Eliezer the son of Rabbi Yosi HaGelili says: if the Angel of Death comes and says to me, 'Why was I created?' I say to him, 'I created you for the nations of the world, if they do not accept My Torah - not for My children'" - so far.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:12: Further, concerning the punishment for unintentional sin, it is explained in the Talmud, Tractate Nazir (23a), of blessed memory: similarly, (Numbers 30:13) "her husband has annulled them, and the Lord will forgive her" - Scripture speaks of a woman whose husband annulled her vow and she did not know it, [teaching] that she requires atonement and forgiveness. And whenever Rabbi Akiva reached this verse he would weep: if one who intended to bring up pork in his hand but brought up lamb requires atonement and forgiveness, how much more so one who intended to bring up pork and did bring up pork! And it says further there: Isi ben Yehudah says, "and he did not know, and is guilty, and shall bear his iniquity" (Leviticus 5:17) - over this matter let all who grieve, grieve - so far.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:13: Further, I found a passage from Tanna DeVei Eliyahu speaking of the matter of fear, which I have chosen to quote here, printed in the Yalkut in the portion of Lech Lecha (remez 76), on the verse (Genesis 15:3) "and Abram said, behold, You have given me no offspring," etc. - his words: "A person should always guard in his heart that no sin, even a minor one, come to him. Go and learn from our first forefathers, who went down to Egypt only because of a minor matter, that Abraham spoke, 'how shall I know?' And as a reward for the small measure of fear that Ishmael showed his father, the Holy One, blessed be He, did not permit any nation or kingdom to rule over his descendants [i.e., Ishmael's]. And as a reward for the two tears that Esau shed, they gave him Mount Seir, from which the rains of blessing never cease. And as a reward for taking his belongings and going away from his brother Jacob, they gave him a hundred provinces. And as a reward for Jacob's listening to Joseph [i.e., a critical remark implied], he was punished for it twenty-two years. And because of the quarrel [at the waters of Meribah], Moses and Aaron were punished. The Sages said: if fire took hold among the moist wood, what will become of the dry? And concerning that time it is said, 'A prayer of Moses.'"
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:14: The Holy One, blessed be He, then returned to appease Moses, and said to him: "Is it not I who said, you are My children and I am your Father? You are My brothers and I am your brother; you are My friends and I am your friend; you are My beloved and I am your beloved. Have I lacked anything from you? I ask of you nothing but this: just as I searched within Myself and found eleven attributes, so I ask of you only eleven attributes" - and these are they (Psalms 15:2) "he who walks blamelessly and does what is right," etc.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:15: Again the Holy One, blessed be He, sought to appease Moses, and said to him: "Is there favoritism before Me, whether Gentile or Israelite, whether man or woman, whether slave or maidservant? Whoever performs a commandment, its reward is alongside it," as it is said (ibid. 36:7) "Your righteousness is like the mighty mountains," etc. From this they said (Bemidbar Rabbah 4:20): whoever increases the honor of Heaven and diminishes his own honor - the honor of Heaven increases and his own honor increases; and whoever diminishes the honor of Heaven and increases his own honor - the honor of Heaven remains in its place and his own honor diminishes.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:16: A story is told of a man who stood in the synagogue with his son standing opposite him; all the congregation would answer "Halleluyah" after the reader, but his son answered with frivolous words. They said to him, "See your son, who answers with frivolous words!" He said to them, "What should I do to him - he's a child, let him play." The next day he did the same, throughout all eight days of the festival, and the father said nothing to him. Before that year, or two years, or three years had passed, that man died, and his wife died, and his son died, and his son's son died, and fifteen souls departed from his household, and only one couple remained to him - one lame and blind, and one imbecile and wicked.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:17: Again, a story is told of a man who regretted that he had not studied Scripture or Mishnah. Once, he was standing in the synagogue, and when the reader before the ark reached the sanctification of the [Divine] Name, he raised his voice and said "Holy, Holy, Holy." They said to him, "Why did you raise your voice?" He said to them, "I did not merit [to study] Scripture or Mishnah, and now that I have been given the opportunity, shall I not raise my voice, that my soul may find satisfaction?" Before that year, or two years, or three years had passed, that man went up from Babylonia to the Land of Israel, and they made him a general of the emperor's army, and appointed him head over all the fortified cities in the Land of Israel; they gave him a place, and he built a city and settled it, and they named it "Colonia" after him, for him, his children, and his children's children, to the end [of the generations].
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:18: A story is told of a certain priest [Kohen] who fed his animal terumah [priestly tithe], and fire fell upon him and consumed thirty bundles [of grain] and thirty garments and twenty-four jars of wine and sixteen jars of oil and the rest of his property. He came and stood before the Sages and told them what had happened to him; he said to them, "I am a priest, and I fed my animal terumah." The Sages heard and said, "Blessed is the Omnipresent, before whom there is no favoritism; behold, terumah and consecrated things that have no eater at all - do they not simply go to be burned?" He said to them, "Have you not taught me that karshinin [a kind of legume] of terumah may be fed to an animal, a wild beast, and chickens?" They said to him, "They only said this of karshinin, which from the start are food for animals; but in a year of famine, people also eat them, and therefore David decreed concerning them [restrictions]." From this they said: whoever feeds his animal terumah, even terumah from outside the Land, of him Scripture says (Proverbs 19:16) "he who despises his ways shall die," and it says (Numbers 18:32) "and you shall not profane the holy things of the children of Israel," etc.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:19: We learn from Abraham that from the very start of his deeds he was in fear before the Holy One, blessed be He, as it is said (Genesis 15:1) "fear not, Abram" - one says "fear not" only to one who truly fears Heaven. They gave a parable for this: to what can this be compared? To a king who said to his son, "Go out and kill these bandits, and if they fall into your hand, do not benefit from their money, so that people should not say the king's son went out to kill these bandits only for the sake of taking the money." He went out and killed them; on his return his father went out to greet him and said to him, "My son, blessed are you, and may you have satisfaction that you did not benefit at all from their money; and now I will pay you from my own treasury - silver and gold, precious stones and pearls, and every desirable vessel in the world." For this reason our father Abraham was compared [in this way]: when he killed the kings, the king of Sodom came out to greet him and said to him, "give me the persons," etc. He said to him, "Fool of the world! Do I need silver and gold, precious stones and pearls, and every desirable vessel from you - from a thread to a shoelace," etc. Therefore it is said, "I am your shield," etc.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:20: We learn from Isaac that from the very start of his deeds he was in fear before the Holy One, blessed be He: Isaac was seventy-five years old when our father Abraham passed away; he said, "Woe is me, perhaps I lack the good deeds that my father had - what will become of me before the Holy One, blessed be He?" Immediately the mercy of the Holy One, blessed be He, was aroused, and He spoke with him that very night, as it is said (Genesis 25:11) "and it came to pass after the death of Abraham," etc.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:21: We learn from Jacob that from the very start of his deeds he feared Heaven, as it is said (ibid. 35:4) "and they gave to Jacob all the foreign gods," etc. And likewise our first forefathers, as it is said (Exodus 14:31) "and Israel saw the great hand," etc. - to teach you that as a reward for the fear and the faith they had at the beginning, the Holy One, blessed be He, will in the future come and redeem them, as it is said (Micah 4:10) "writhe and travail, daughter of Zion," etc. - so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:22: Concerning the matter of fear of sin, Rashbi, peace be upon him, explains further (Zohar, Bereishit 7b) - his words: "Why is it called 'the fear of the Lord'? Because it is the tree of good and evil - if a person merits, behold, it is good; and if he does not merit, behold, it is evil - and therefore fear dwells in this place, and this is the gate leading upward to all the good of the world" - so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:23: The intent of his saying "Why is it called 'the fear of the Lord'" is to ask two things: first, concerning the existence of fear in this place [Malchut]; and second, what connection the two words "fear of the Lord" have - why not simply say "fear of God" [yirat Elohim]? And he answered, "because it is the tree of good and evil." My teacher, peace be upon him, explains in his commentary on the Sabba, that this attribute [Malchut] is called "the tree of knowledge of good and evil" because it draws from the depth of good and the depth of evil, which are Chesed and Din [kindness and judgment]; and also because beneath it are good and evil. It is explained in the Tikkunim (90b): "the tree of knowledge of good" - this is Metatron; "and evil" - this is Samael. And the verse says (Deuteronomy 30:15) "See, I have set before you today life and good, and death and evil" - life is bound to good, and death is bound to evil, and two paths branch out from it below, and therefore this is the place of free choice, and it is written "and you shall choose life." If a person merits through his deeds, he cleaves to the good, which is YHVH, the Tree of Life, the side of kindness and mercy, that is (Psalms 145:9) "the Lord is good to all, and His mercies," etc.; and likewise YHVH [numerically] equals "good" [tov] when spelled in full [via a particular method]. But if he does not merit, he cleaves to the evil, which is death, and these are the outer kelipot [shells].
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:24: With this, both fine points are resolved: one must fear, because beneath it is evil, lest his soul cleave to evil - for death and the evil to which it cleaves become part of his soul after his departure from the world, along the lines of what is explained in the Zohar (portion of Korach, 177a), on the verse (Job 34:11) "for according to the deed of a man He repays him." So too, he should not cause this attribute [Malchut] to cleave to evil, God forbid, as will be further explained regarding the blemish a person can cause to the [divine] attributes, blessed be He. And likewise, "the fear of the Lord" - if he is God-fearing, he merits cleaving to YHVH, which is good, and his soul, after departing from the world, cleaves to the good - that is, the good hidden away for the righteous in the Garden of Eden; and "God saw the light, that it was good" - for YHVH is the source of all good in the world. This he made precise when he said, "this is the gate leading in to all the good of the world." The word "good" is along the lines of "there is nothing higher than delight," and also the word "good" includes all the good found in all the [divine] attributes; and this is YHVH, the sum total of the ten attributes in direct light, which is kindness and mercy, as is explained in the Tikkunim (6b).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:25: Now, man is composed of good and evil, which are the good inclination and the evil inclination; and if a person merits subduing the evil inclination within him, he causes the subduing of the powers of judgment and the kelipot, and causes the drawing forth of good upon him. This is the precise meaning of "if a person merits" - for man is composed of good and evil, and must strengthen the good inclination over the evil inclination; and if, God forbid, he does the opposite, he blemishes the supernal roots, for judgment is not [meant to be] included apart from being subsumed under kindness.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:26: This is explained in the Zohar (Vaera 26b), on the verse (Deuteronomy 4:39) "and you shall know this day and take it to your heart" - their words: "Rabbi Elazar said further: the wicked cause a blemish above. What is this blemish? That the left is not included in the right, that the evil inclination is not included in the good inclination, because of the sins of human beings, and they cause a blemish only to themselves, in fact - this is [the meaning of] what is written (Deuteronomy 32:5) 'corruption is His, not His children's, is their blemish' - as it were, they act [as if to blemish Him] yet they do not [truly] act [upon Him] - they act so that the blessings from above are not drawn down upon them, as it says (ibid. 11:17) 'and He will restrain the heavens and there will be no rain'; but they do not act [upon Him Himself], for the heavens take for themselves the blessings they need, and only fail to draw them down below. Certainly, the blemish is that of these wicked ones themselves. Further, [the word] 'Lo' [to Him, not] is spelled with a Vav, [meaning] that the right is not included in the left, so that blessings are not drawn down below; ['Lo'] is [also] spelled with an Aleph, [meaning] that they do not take [the blessings] to draw them down below. Who causes this? Because the wicked separate the evil inclination from the good inclination and cleave to the evil inclination" - so far, as relevant to us.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:27: Our intent here is clear, but let us nonetheless explain the matter of the blemish he speaks of, "they act and they do not act." The meaning is that Rabbi Elazar found the plain sense of the verse difficult: for according to the apparent reading, "corruption is His, not" would mean that no blemish at all reaches Him, blessed be He, from our deeds, but rather "their blemish is His children's" - meaning the blemish and defect belong to the children who commit that blemish and sin; if so, the verse should simply be silent [on this point] and say "His children's is their blemish, a perverse and crooked generation." For this reason he explained that the meaning is "corruption is His" - that a blemish does reach Him, but it is not a complete blemish, and this is [why it is spelled] "Lo" with an Aleph [i.e., a partial negation]; but the complete blemish and defect belongs to the children who commit it - "His children's is their blemish" [mumam, in the plural, complete form]. Therefore, in what pertains to Him he said "corruption" [shichet], which is a minor diminishment, but what pertains to the children is a complete "blemish" [mum]. With this we understand the words of Rabbi Elazar, peace be upon him, who said "the wicked cause a blemish above," etc., and said afterward "and they cause a blemish only to themselves, in fact" - that the actual blemish is upon them.
